title: Agentic Enterprise - What your CEO must know about AI -  Hubert Misztela

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk centers on how AI agents are structured and deployed across enterprises, covering agent definition, multi-agent swarms, planning, and harness architecture. The content addresses internal enterprise workflows, organizational transformation, and knowledge work through AI agents. The talk focuses on strategic planning for agent deployment and the cultural adoption challenges enterprises face. The content is pitched at executives and practitioners without requiring deep technical prerequisites. This is a conference presentation delivered at AI Engineer World's Fair 2025. All cited claims are directly stated in the transcript with no external verification.

summary: Hubert Misztela leads AI research in drug design at Novartis and presents a framework for how AI agents will transform large organizations. He provocatively claims organizations may be run by AI agents within three years. AI agents are defined as LLM-based applications exhibiting autonomy through step-by-step planning, tool usage, and dynamic action adjusted by previous outcomes. Key capabilities include reasoning, multi-step planning, adaptability, persistent memory, contextual retrieval (RAG), interactive sandboxes, and computer-using agents. Misztela urges companies to evolve every digital asset into an agent-accessible tool. From a workflow perspective, he distinguishes automation (substituting a step) from augmentation (doing it faster/better), noting agentic workflows where agents handle broader cognitive tasks and serve as glue between steps, reducing human intervention to feedback moments. A critical first step is identifying workflows and their deep context—often undocumented, existing only in employees' heads. He introduces five personas (silent achiever, individual contributor, connector, multiplier, knowledge hub) rather than job titles for better agent deployment decisions. Projecting agents onto workflows shows steps merging, multipliers' impact magnified, and knowledge hubs most prone to substitution. Ambiguous, situation-dependent workflows remain better suited for humans; subjectivity can be a feature, not a bug. Misztela identifies emerging patterns: intelligence and domain knowledge are commoditizing, ceasing to be competitive advantages. Context understanding gains value. AI supercharges 'doers'—potentially producing 100x engineers with less middle ground, creating polarization. New roles emerge in AI-mature organizations like workflow miners and human-AI orchestrators. He outlines a democratization progression: general assistants, individual assistants with memory, employee-built agents (requiring cognitive self-awareness to articulate internal steps), digital twins for knowledge retention, multi-employee agents, and agent swarms. Challenges include adoption culture (are we ready for agents to delegate subtasks to humans?) and ethics of autonomy (defining values for agents, resolving human-AI conflicts). He closes with a strategy test: if swapping 'AI agent' with 'machine learning' or 'data' leaves your strategy unchanged, it's already outdated.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and AI Agent Definition
sections.summary: Misztela introduces himself as Novartis AI drug design lead and defines AI agents as LLM-based applications with autonomous multi-step planning, dynamic tool use, and adaptability. He lists key capabilities including reasoning, persistent memory, RAG, interactive workspaces, and computer-using agents, urging organizations to convert digital assets into agent tools.

sections.title: Workflow Perspective: Automation vs Augmentation
sections.summary: Explains workflows as process execution with sequential steps. Distinguishes automation (substituting steps) from augmentation (doing steps better/faster). The new differentiator is agentic workflows where LLMs handle broader cognitive tasks and serve as glue between steps, reducing human intervention to feedback moments. First takeaway: identify workflows and their deep, often undocumented context.

sections.title: Network Perspective and Persona Archetypes
sections.summary: Argues job titles are insufficient for AI planning. Introduces five personas—silent achiever, individual contributor, connector, multiplier, knowledge hub—as better archetypes for understanding employee contributions and projecting agent impact at organizational scale.

sections.title: Projecting AI Agents onto Workflows
sections.summary: Demonstrates how agents transform workflows: coding assistants let silent achievers merge steps, multipliers' impact extends to entire teams, and knowledge hubs become most prone to substitution. Emphasizes analyzing patterns across all company workflows to identify which agents to build.

sections.title: Emerging Patterns: Commoditization and New Roles
sections.summary: Discusses human vs agent task allocation: subjectivity can be a feature keeping humans in place, while repetitive well-defined tasks suit agents. Intelligence and domain knowledge commoditize, ceasing to be competitive edges. Employees must pivot to multidisciplinary or deeper specialization. Senior engineers pulled to work directly with domain experts. Context understanding gains value. AI supercharges doers—potentially 100x engineers with polarization. New roles emerge: workflow miners, human-AI orchestrators.

sections.title: Democratizing Agent Adoption
sections.summary: Outlines a step-by-step democratization progression: general assistants, individual assistants with memory and personal context, employee-built agents using no-code/low-code tools (requiring cognitive self-awareness to articulate internal workflow steps), digital twins for retaining organizational knowledge when employees leave, multi-employee agents serving whole teams, and agent swarms. Software stack maturity around LLMs enables all of this now.

sections.title: Challenges: Adoption and Ethics of Autonomy
sections.summary: Addresses challenges beyond technical ones (groundedness, hallucinations, guardrails, security): adoption and ethics. References DeepMind AGI levels table—question of whether organizations are socially ready for agents to delegate subtasks to humans. Ethics of autonomy requires explicitly defining values for agents despite human disagreement, and resolving human-AI conflicts, possibly with justice agents. Quotes John Cenox on machine freedom requiring moral standards.

sections.title: Opportunities and Executive Summary
sections.summary: Lists opportunities including synthetic reality simulation before real-world activity, regulatory loophole finding, and M&A scouting. Executive summary: if swapping 'AI agent' with 'machine learning' or 'data' leaves strategy unchanged, it's outdated. Agents bring new capabilities; detailed workflow understanding is crucial; democratize agents; use network personas; prepare for rapid transformation and org chart changes; shift mindset for technology that may lead us; ethics remains crucial.
